transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Yeah, I... I guess I'm here because I just can't seem to shake this... this thing that's happening in my head. I'm a courier, you know, a messenger, so I'm always running around the city, in and out of lobbies, picking things up. It's usually just autopilot for me, I've done it a million times. 

But recently, what brings me in is that I keep getting these... these intense flashes. They just hit me completely out of nowhere. I'll just be standing at a pickup counter, right? Just waiting for a receptionist to hand me an envelope or sign a slip, totally normal day, and suddenly it's like I'm not even at work anymore. I'm right back in that crowded holding room. 

It's so real, man. I can see that fight breaking out all over again right in front of me, and I can hear... God, the sound is so loud... I can hear everybody getting violently shoved up against the wall. Like, the actual physical thud of bodies hitting the wall and the yelling. And I'm just standing there in some random office building with my messenger bag, but my brain is completely back in that room, seeing the whole thing happen again. It just hits me so hard out of the blue, and I can't stop it from taking over.
When these flashbacks happen, do you ever feel like you're outside of your body watching yourself, or like the world around you isn't real?

Outside my body? Like... like watching myself from the ceiling or something? No, man, no, I don't get that at all. Honestly, it's... it's kind of the exact opposite, if that makes any sense. I don't feel disconnected or like I'm floating around. I am so intensely, painfully stuck right inside my own skin when it hits. 

Like, I can feel the exact weight of my canvas bag strap digging into my collarbone, and I can feel my own hands gripping the edge of whatever reception desk I'm at, just holding on for dear life. I'm completely me, looking out of my own two eyes. It's just that what those eyes are seeing is... is that holding room again. So, the world around me—the actual lobby I'm standing in—it doesn't feel fake, exactly, it just gets completely drowned out. The memory is so loud and so heavy that it just paints over reality. 

I'm not watching a movie of myself. I'm right there, bracing myself, feeling every single thing. I mean, honestly, I wish I could float outside my body when it happens. Maybe it wouldn't be so terrifying if I could just detach from it, you know? But no, I'm trapped right inside myself, feeling the whole thing happen all over again.
Since these flashbacks started, have you been feeling on edge, like you're constantly in danger, or have trouble calming down?

Yeah, "on edge" is... I mean, that's putting it mildly. I feel like my nerves are just completely, absolutely fried. Because, you know, being a courier, I'm out in the city all day, every day, and the city is just... it's loud. It's always loud. I used to just tune it out, it was just background noise, part of the job. 

But now? Now it's like every single sudden noise is a direct threat. Like, if my dispatcher's radio crackles—just a standard static crackle on my shoulder—or if a police siren suddenly blares from a couple of streets over, or even if I'm just walking past a storefront and somebody lets a heavy door slam shut behind them... I mean, I jump so hard. I literally, physically jump, like I'm about to get rushed by someone. Like somebody is coming right at me out of my blind spot to tackle me or something. 

And it's not just the jumping, it's... it's how I feel afterward, you know? Because I can't just laugh it off or shake it off like a normal person getting startled. My heart just starts pounding. I mean pounding so incredibly hard, like it's going to crack my ribs open, and it just keeps going and going. I can't calm down. It gets so bad that I actually have to stop what I'm doing. I'll have to physically pull my bike over to the curb, or if I'm in a building making a delivery, I have to immediately step outside. I just have to get out and stand there on the pavement, gripping my bag, just trying to convince my body that I'm not under attack. And it takes so long for my heart rate to just go back to normal. It's exhausting, it really is, just constantly walking around bracing myself, waiting for the next loud noise to happen.
